title: Raspberry Jam
subtitle: Bright, lightly set raspberry jam with whole fruit
excerpt: Raspberry jam sets faster than almost any other fruit jam because raspberries are naturally high in pectin. Twenty minutes from pan to jar, and the flavour stays clean and sharp.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton (1861) and Pam Corbin in Preserves both use this recipe. Raspberry sets faster than any other common jam fruit and needs no added pectin.

recipe.batchNotes: Up to 2 kg fruit at once. Beyond that, even raspberries slow to set.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Sterilise jars ahead; the jam itself is fast enough to make in one go.

glossaryTerms.definition: The temperature at which jam will set when cooled, typically 104–105 °C. Confirmed by the wrinkle test on a chilled plate.

content.text: Raspberry jam sets faster than almost any other home preserve. The fruit has enough natural pectin to set without added lemon juice. The short cooking time keeps the colour vivid and the flavour bright. Makes about three 450 g jars.

items.prepNote: warmed in a low oven for 10 minutes if possible

content.text: Warmed sugar dissolves faster and cuts the total cooking time. Three sterilised 450 g jars.

Put the raspberries in the jam pan over low heat. As they begin to release juice, add the warmed sugar and stir until completely dissolved. Check by tilting the pan,  the base should look clear. This takes about 5 minutes.
Raise the heat and bring to a full rolling boil,  a boil that cannot be stirred down. Cook without stirring for 8 to 10 minutes. Put a plate in the freezer. At 104 (the
) °C (or after 8 minutes), test on the cold plate: push the surface with your fingertip. If it wrinkles, the jam is ready. If it runs, boil for 2 more minutes and test again.
Skim the foam. Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then ladle into hot sterilised jars and seal immediately.

items.symptom: Jam is too thick — nearly solid in the jar
items.cause: Overcooked or too much sugar relative to fruit weight.
items.fix: Next time weigh the fruit after washing and match the sugar to that weight. If the jam has set too firm in the jar, it still tastes good, warm it slightly to loosen for spreading.

items.cause: Some sugar was still undissolved before boiling, or the jam was cooked too long.
items.fix: Always make sure every sugar crystal has dissolved before raising the heat. If the finished jam crystallises in storage, warm the jar in a bowl of hot water and stir.

items.cause: Too long on the heat, raspberry colour degrades with prolonged cooking.
items.fix: The shorter the boil the better. Have everything ready before you start so you don't idle on the stove.

items.cause: Fruit was underripe or the boil didn't reach 104 °C.
items.fix: Return the jam to the pan, add the juice of 1 lemon, boil again and test. Underripe fruit has more pectin, so if anything overripe fruit is the culprit here.

content.text: 12 months sealed. Use within a month once opened and refrigerate.
